# Introduction to containers {.unnumbered}

> *"A virtual machine is taken to be an efficient, isolated duplicate of the
> real machine."* — Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, 1974 [@popek1974]

This part corresponds to the fifth course of the master: a short, single-module
introduction to **containers** and to their **orchestration**. The first four
parts produced programs and models that run on one machine — the author's.
This part is about the step that comes next for every program that matters:
running it somewhere else, identically, many times, and keeping it running.

The single chapter follows the course's lessons — what containers and
orchestration are, the foundations of containers, running a container with
Docker, orchestrating containers with Kubernetes — and goes beneath each of
them: the kernel mechanisms a container is made of, the image format and its
hashes, the build cache, signals and exit codes, the control loops of
Kubernetes and the bounds that govern a rolling update.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this part matters for an AI engineer
A model is useful only where it runs, and it runs only if its whole stack —
interpreter, numerical libraries, the serialised model, the serving code —
arrives intact. Containers are how models are shipped today: training jobs on
GPU clusters, batch scoring pipelines and prediction services are container
images scheduled by an orchestrator. Knowing what an image contains, why a
build is slow or an image is huge, why a container takes ten seconds to stop
or dies with code 137, and how an update can avoid dropping requests is part
of the job of putting machine learning into production.
:::

## What you will be able to do {.unnumbered}

1. Explain what a container is, build one by hand from namespaces, a root
   filesystem and cgroups, and predict how CPU is shared among containers by
   weights and quotas (@sec-ctr-what, @sec-ctr-kernel).
2. Read an OCI image — index, manifest, configuration, layers — and use
   digests correctly; explain why deleting a file never shrinks an image,
   and build reproducible images (@sec-ctr-images).
3. Write Dockerfiles that rebuild fast and ship small, using the cache's
   prefix property, the optimal order of steps and multi-stage builds
   (@sec-ctr-build).
4. Run containers safely: ports, volumes, environment, non-root users,
   read-only filesystems, limits, graceful shutdown and the meaning of exit
   codes (@sec-ctr-run).
5. Deploy, heal, scale and update a service on Kubernetes, and bound the
   duration of a rolling update (@sec-ctr-k8s).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

From Part I: virtual environments and pinned dependencies
(@sec-ch-venv, @sec-requirements), files and JSON (@sec-ch-files),
exceptions (@sec-ch-exceptions). From Part II: compiling and linking
(@sec-toolchain) and, above all, processes, signals and exit statuses
(@sec-ch-cpp-python). From Parts III and IV: pipelines that avoid leakage
(@sec-leakage) and the models that the examples serve. Probability at the
level of Part III (independence, expectation, the union bound) is enough for
the proofs. This part does not repeat any of it: it links back.

To run the examples you need a Linux machine (or a Linux VM, which Docker
Desktop provides on macOS and Windows) with Docker Engine and, for the last
section, a small Kubernetes such as k3s, kind or minikube.

## Graded practice {.unnumbered}

As in Part IV, every main section ends with a **Practice** block of three
exercises — **Easy** (by hand), **Medium** (in code), **Hard** (a small open
problem) — each with a collapsed hint and a separate collapsed solution, with
executed code. Since this course has no final project, the Hard exercises
follow a common thread instead: **putting a trained model into production** —
a wine classifier like those of Parts III and IV, trained at build time,
served over HTTP, scored in batch, rolled out on a cluster.

## Tools and versions {.unnumbered}

The examples were executed with **Docker Engine 29.9.3** (BuildKit via buildx 0.38.1, Compose 5.7.0), **runc 1.5.2** and **k3s v1.37.2+k3s1** (Kubernetes v1.37.2), on a 2-CPU virtual machine with 7 GB of RAM, Linux 6.18.44, cgroup v1; every output shown was produced by actually running it when the book was built.


The standards referred to are the OCI Image Format Specification 1.1
[@oci2025image] and Runtime Specification 1.3 [@oci2025runtime]. The build
machine could not reach public image registries; the Dockerfiles therefore
take their base image as a build argument with the official image as default
(for example `ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim`), and the book builds them with local
equivalents produced from the Ubuntu 24.04 archive. The helper that runs the
examples and masks machine-specific output is
[`containers/ctrbook.py`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-engineering-handbook/blob/main/containers/ctrbook.py).

The data are the wine measurements that ship with scikit-learn
[@aeberhard1992] (UCI, CC BY 4.0).

## Map of the part {.unnumbered}

| Section | Core topics | What the book adds |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-ctr-what | containers versus virtual machines and virtual environments, images, runtimes, registries, orchestration | measured start-up time, the history from `chroot` to the OCI |
| @sec-ctr-kernel | namespaces, root filesystems, cgroups, union filesystems | a container built by hand; weighted fair sharing and quotas proved and measured; the v1→v2 weight conversion |
| @sec-ctr-images | the OCI image: index, manifest, configuration, layers; tags and digests | collision bound for SHA-256, Merkle commitment, additive layers and leaked secrets, reproducible digests |
| @sec-ctr-build | Dockerfile, build context, cache, multi-stage builds | prefix property, expected rebuild cost and optimal order proved by an exchange argument, static C++ on `scratch` |
| @sec-ctr-run | life cycle, ports, volumes, environment, users, signals, exit codes | PID 1 and `SIGTERM` measured, the ambiguity of 137, a locked-down batch job and its OOM kill |
| @sec-ctr-k8s | Kubernetes objects, deployments, services, probes, scaling, rolling updates | reconciliation loops, bounds on rolling updates, the autoscaler's fixed point, a zero-downtime update measured |

## No final project {.unnumbered}

This course has **no final project**, so this part ends with its chapter's
synthesis exercises instead of a project chapter. The "In the projects" box of
the chapter applies the techniques to the projects of the earlier parts — the
phone book of Part I, the CRM of Part II, the classifier of Part IV — and Part
VI continues the same thread by giving the model a proper web API.
